chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Overview

Quick-reference for the query shapes used throughout this manual. MySQL syntax shown; dialect differences flagged inline where they matter most; Appendix B covers the rest in full.
Basics
```sql
SELECT col1, col2 FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY col1 LIMIT 10;
SELECT DISTINCT col FROM table;
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(col), COUNT(DISTINCT col) FROM table;
SELECT * FROM table WHERE col IS NULL;              -- never = NULL
SELECT * FROM table WHERE col BETWEEN a AND b;       -- inclusive both ends
SELECT * FROM table WHERE col IN (1, 2, 3);
SELECT * FROM table WHERE col LIKE 'A%' ESCAPE '\\'; -- % any chars, _ one char
```

Joins
```sql
SELECT * FROM a JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id;                          -- inner: matched rows only
SELECT * FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id;                      -- keep all of a
SELECT * FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id WHERE b.id IS NULL;   -- anti-join: a with no match
SELECT * FROM a JOIN a b ON b.parent_id = a.id;                    -- self join, alias mandatory
```

Aggregation
```sql
SELECT col, COUNT(*), SUM(amt), AVG(amt), MIN(amt), MAX(amt)
FROM   t GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;                         -- HAVING filters groups, WHERE filters rows
SELECT col, SUM(CASE WHEN status='x' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM t GROUP BY col;  -- conditional count
```

Duplicates and orphans
```sql
SELECT key_col, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY key_col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;         -- duplicates
SELECT a.* FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id WHERE a.fk IS NOT NULL AND b.id IS NULL;  -- orphans
```

Subqueries / CTEs
```sql
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col > (SELECT AVG(col) FROM t);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE u.t_id = t.id);
WITH x AS (SELECT ... ) SELECT * FROM x WHERE ...;
```

Window functions
```sql
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY dt DESC) rn FROM t;    -- latest per group: WHERE rn=1
SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY val DESC) FROM t;                             -- ties share rank, skips numbers
SELECT *, LAG(val) OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY dt) prev FROM t;
SELECT *, SUM(val) OVER (ORDER BY dt) running_total FROM t;
```

```sql
Set operators
SELECT a FROM t1 UNION ALL SELECT a FROM t2;         -- stack, keep duplicates (default choice)
SELECT a FROM t1 EXCEPT SELECT a FROM t2;             -- in t1 not t2 (MySQL 8.0.31+)
```

DML
```sql
INSERT INTO t (col1, col2) VALUES (v1, v2);
UPDATE t SET col = val WHERE id = 1;
DELETE FROM t WHERE id = 1;
START TRANSACTION; ... ROLLBACK; / COMMIT;
```

| Schema inspection | SHOW CREATE TABLE t\G |
|---|---|
| SELECT * FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=DATABASE() AND table_name='t'; | EXPLAIN SELECT ...; |

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Overview

| Task | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| Limit rows | LIMIT 5 | LIMIT 5 | TOP 5 / OFFSET...FETCH |
| Pagination | LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 | LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 | OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH NEXT 5 ROWS ONLY |
| Current date/time | CURRENT_DATE, NOW() | CURRENT_DATE, NOW() | CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE), GETDATE() |
| Add interval | DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY) | d + INTERVAL '7 days' | DATEADD(day, 7, d) |
| Date diff | DATEDIFF(end, start) (days) | end - start | DATEDIFF(day, start, end) (note arg order) |
| String concat | CONCAT(a,b) | a \|\| b | a + b / CONCAT(a,b) |
| Concat with separator | CONCAT_WS(' ',a,b) | CONCAT_WS(' ',a,b) | CONCAT_WS(' ',a,b) |
| String length (chars) | CHAR_LENGTH(x) | LENGTH(x) | LEN(x) (ignores trailing spaces) |
| Substring | SUBSTRING(x,2,3) | SUBSTRING(x,2,3) | SUBSTRING(x,2,3) |
| Case-insensitive match | collation-dependent, LOWER() | ILIKE, LOWER() | collation-dependent, LOWER() |
| Auto-increment PK | AUTO_INCREMENT | SERIAL / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY | IDENTITY(1,1) |
| Upsert | ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE | ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE | MERGE |
| Row-limiting delete | DELETE ... LIMIT n | not supported directly | not supported directly |
| String aggregation | GROUP_CONCAT(x ORDER BY y SEPARATOR ',') | STRING_AGG(x, ',' ORDER BY y) | STRING_AGG(x, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY y) |
| CTE | WITH x AS (...) (8.0+) | WITH x AS (...) | ;WITH x AS (...) if mid-batch |
| Recursive CTE | WITH RECURSIVE | WITH RECURSIVE | WITH (no keyword needed) |
| Set operators | UNION, UNION ALL (INTERSECT/EXCEPT 8.0.31+) | full set | full set |
| Window functions | 8.0+ | full support | 2005+ (frames 2012+) |
| NULL-safe equals | <=> | IS NOT DISTINCT FROM | IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (2022+) |
| Boolean type | TINYINT(1) | BOOLEAN | BIT |
| Quote identifiers | `backticks` | "double quotes" | [brackets] |
| Quote strings | 'single quotes' (also " unless ANSI_QUOTES) | 'single quotes' only | 'single quotes' only |
| Sample rows (top-of-table peek) | SELECT * FROM t LIMIT 10 | SELECT * FROM t LIMIT 10 | SELECT TOP 10 * FROM t |
| Explain plan | EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) | EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) | "Actual execution plan" (SSMS) |
| Regex match | REGEXP | ~ | not native (LIKE classes only) |
| JSON extract | JSON_EXTRACT(x,'$.a') / ->> | x->>'a' | JSON_VALUE(x,'$.a') |
| Schema = database? | Yes, synonyms | No, schema is inside a database (public default) | No, schema inside a database (dbo default) |
| Sequence generator | recursive CTE | generate_series(a,b) | recursive CTE or sys.all_objects cross join |
| Raise a custom error | SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT='...' | RAISE EXCEPTION '...' | THROW 50000, '...', 1 |
| DDL in a transaction | No (implicit commit) | Yes | Yes (if batch wrapped) |
| Disable a trigger | no session switch | ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER | DISABLE TRIGGER ... ON ... |

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Overview

ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability; the four guarantees a transaction provides (7.7).
 Aggregate function — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; collapses many rows into one value (3.1).
 Alias — A short name given to a table or column, used to disambiguate or shorten references (e for employees).
 Anti-join — A join pattern (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS) that finds rows with no match in another table (4.1).
 ANSI SQL / standard SQL — The vendor-neutral specification that MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server each implement with local extensions.
 Atomicity — All statements in a transaction succeed together or none do (7.3).
 Autocommit — A client mode where every statement is its own transaction, committed immediately.
 B-tree — The typical internal structure of a database index; a sorted, balanced search tree.
 Cardinality — The number of distinct values in a column, or the number of rows on each side of a relationship (one-to-many, etc.).
 Cartesian product — Every row of one table paired with every row of another; the result of a CROSS JOIN or a forgotten WHERE in comma-join syntax (4.1).
 CDC (Change Data Capture) — Streaming a table's inserts/updates/deletes to another system in near real time (mentioned in ETL contexts).
 Check constraint — A rule on a column or row that must evaluate true for every insert/update (8.1).
 Collation — The rules governing string comparison and sorting: case sensitivity, accent sensitivity, character ordering (2.5).
 Column — One named, typed attribute of a table (1.1).
 Composite key — A primary or unique key made of more than one column.
 Constraint — A database-enforced rule: primary key, foreign key, unique, not null, check (8.1).
 Correlated subquery — A subquery that references a column from the outer query, conceptually re-evaluated per outer row (5.1).
 Covering index — An index containing every column a query needs, so the table itself need not be read.
 CTE (Common Table Expression) — A named, one-statement-scoped subquery defined with WITH (5.2).
 DDL (Data Definition Language) — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE; statements that change structure (0.2, 7.4).
 Deadlock — Two transactions each waiting on a lock the other holds; the database kills one to break the cycle (7.7).
 DECIMAL / NUMERIC — An exact fixed-point numeric type, required for money (1.2).
 Derived table — A subquery used in place of a table in FROM, requiring an alias (5.1).
 DML (Data Manipulation Language) — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; statements that change data (0.2, 7.1).
 Durability — Once committed, data survives a crash (7.7).
 ENUM — A column type restricted to a fixed list of allowed text values (1.2, 8.4).
 ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) — The process of moving and reshaping data between systems (6.1).
 Fan-out — Row duplication caused by a one-to-many join, inflating counts and sums if not accounted for (4.1).
 Foreign key (FK) — A column whose values must exist as a key in another table, enforcing referential integrity (4.3, 8.1).
 Idempotent — An operation that has the same effect whether run once or many times (7.2, 7.7).
 Index — A sorted auxiliary structure that speeds up row lookup at the cost of slower writes and extra storage (8.1).
 Isolation level — The degree to which concurrent transactions are shielded from each other's uncommitted work (7.7).
 Join — Combining rows from two or more tables based on a related column (4.1).
 Lock — A hold a transaction takes on a row (or table) to prevent conflicting concurrent changes (7.7).
 Logical orphan — A child row whose parent still technically exists (satisfying the foreign key) but is soft-deleted or otherwise "gone" in business terms (4.3).
 Lost update — A concurrency bug where two transactions each read-then-write a value, and the second write silently overwrites the first (7.7).
 Materialized view — A view whose result is physically stored and must be refreshed, unlike an ordinary view which re-runs its query each time (8.3).
 Migration — Either (a) moving data from one system/schema to another (6.1), or (b) a versioned script that changes database structure (6.4). Context disambiguates.
 MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) — A technique letting readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers (7.7).
 Normalization — Organizing data to minimize redundancy, typically by splitting it across related tables (0.7, out of this manual's scope as a design discipline).
 NULL — The marker for "no value" / unknown; behaves specially in comparisons, aggregates and joins (2.3).
 ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) — A code library that translates between application objects and SQL, sometimes hiding the underlying queries.
 Orphan record — A child row referencing a parent that doesn't exist (4.3).
 Partition (window function) — The grouping applied by PARTITION BY inside an OVER() clause, without collapsing rows (5.5). (Distinct from database table partitioning, not covered in this manual.)
 Phantom read — A transaction re-runs a query and gets a different set of rows than before, because rows were inserted or deleted by another transaction in between (7.7).
 Primary key (PK) — A column (or set of columns) uniquely identifying each row; cannot be NULL (8.1).
 Read replica — A copy of a database receiving continuous updates from a primary, accepting only read queries (11.2).
 Referential integrity — The guarantee that foreign key values always point to an existing parent row (0.1, 4.3).
 Sargable — A predicate written so the database can use an index to evaluate it, as opposed to wrapping the column in a function (2.1).
 Schema — Depending on database: (MySQL) a synonym for database; (PostgreSQL/SQL Server) a namespace within a database grouping tables (1.1). Also used informally to mean "the structure of the database" overall.
 Schema drift — Structural or reference-data differences between environments that should match (6.5).
 Scalar subquery — A subquery returning exactly one row and one column, usable anywhere a single value is expected (5.1).
 Self join — A join where a table is joined to itself via aliases, used for hierarchies, pairs, and overlap checks (4.2).
 Snapshot (before/after) — A saved copy of data taken before a change, compared against an "after" copy to isolate exactly what changed (6.6).
 Soft delete — Marking a row as deleted (a flag or timestamp) rather than physically removing it (4.3, 8.4).
 Sanity check / sanity suite — A named, reusable query that returns violating rows for one business rule, run repeatedly to catch regressions (10.2).
 Transaction — A group of statements executed as a single all-or-nothing unit (7.3).
 Trigger — A stored routine that runs automatically in response to a table event (8.3).
 Unique constraint — A rule that no two rows may share the same value (or combination of values) in specified columns; unlike a PK, the column(s) may be nullable (8.1).
 View — A saved, named query that can be queried like a table (8.3).
 Window function — A calculation performed across a set of related rows (a "window") without collapsing them into one output row (5.5).

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Overview

| Error (MySQL, illustrative) | Meaning | Typical fix | 1054: Unknown column 'x' in 'field list' | Column name doesn't exist (typo, wrong table, dropped column) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DESCRIBE table; to check real names (1.1) | 1146: Table 'db.t' doesn't exist | Wrong table name or wrong database selected | SHOW TABLES;, check USE database; | 1064: You have an error in your SQL syntax |
| Missing comma/quote/keyword | Check exactly where the error points | 1052: Column 'x' is ambiguous | Same column name exists in two joined tables | Qualify with alias.column (4.1) |
| 1242: Subquery returns more than 1 row | A scalar-context subquery returned multiple rows | Use IN/EXISTS, or add a filter that guarantees one row (5.1) | 1111: Invalid use of group function | Aggregate used in WHERE, or nested aggregate (AVG(SUM(...))) |
| Move to HAVING; wrap the inner aggregate in a derived table/CTE (3.1, 5.1) | 1055 / ER_WRONG_FIELD_WITH_GROUP: non-aggregated column not in GROUP BY | ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode caught a mixed SELECT list | Add the column to GROUP BY or wrap it in an aggregate (3.2) | 1062: Duplicate entry '...' for key '...' |
| A UNIQUE/PRIMARY constraint was violated | Check for an existing row first, or handle the conflict (upsert, 7.1); named constraints give clearer messages (8.1) | 1048: Column 'x' cannot be null | Insert/update omitted a required value | Supply a value, or check whether the column should be nullable |
| 1364: Field 'x' doesn't have a default value | Required column omitted with no default, strict mode | Include the column in the INSERT | 1406: Data too long for column 'x' | Value exceeds VARCHAR(n)/similar limit, strict mode |
| Shorten the value, or the column may need widening (1.2, 8.2) | 1265: Data truncated for column 'x' | Value doesn't fit the type cleanly (e.g., string into a narrowed ENUM/numeric) | Check the mapping; may indicate a migration issue (6.1, 6.4) | 1452: Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails |
| Insert/update references a parent row that doesn't exist | Verify the parent exists first (4.3) | 1451: Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails | Deleting a parent that still has children | Delete children first, or the constraint's ON DELETE action needs review (4.3, 7.1) |
| 3819: Check constraint 'x' is violated | A CHECK constraint rejected the row | Value must satisfy the rule; check whether the pre-existing data was validated when the constraint was added (6.4, 8.1) | 1205: Lock wait timeout exceeded | Another transaction is holding a lock on the row(s) you need |
| Find and resolve the blocking session (SHOW PROCESSLIST, innodb_trx); check for a forgotten open transaction (7.3, 7.7) | 1213: Deadlock found when trying to get lock | Two transactions blocked each other in a cycle | The database killed one automatically; the application should retry (7.7) | 1093: You can't specify target table 'x' for update in FROM clause |
| MySQL forbids selecting from the table you're updating/deleting, in certain forms | Wrap the inner query in a derived table (5.1) | 1701: Cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint | TRUNCATE blocked by a child relationship, even on an empty child table | Use DELETE instead, or truncate children first (7.4) |
| 3593: You cannot use the window function '...' in this context | A window function was used in WHERE/HAVING/GROUP BY directly | Compute it in a CTE/subquery and filter in the outer query (5.5) | 1248: Every derived table must have its own alias | A subquery in FROM had no alias |
| Add AS alias_name | 1222: The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns | Mismatched column counts across a UNION/EXCEPT/INTERSECT | Line up the column lists exactly (5.4) | PostgreSQL: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block |
| A prior statement in the same transaction errored, and PostgreSQL won't run anything else until you ROLLBACK | ROLLBACK; then retry cleanly (7.3) | Query OK, 0 rows affected on an expected UPDATE | WHERE matched no rows, or matched rows already had that value ("Matched" vs "Changed", 7.1) | Re-check the WHERE with a SELECT first |

practical.pass: You apply SQL Interview Questions for QA Roles on the sample database (or a tagged QA row) and can say what empty vs non-empty results mean.
practical.fail: You copy a blog query, skip SQL Interview Questions for QA Roles, or treat a UI success toast as proof the row is correct.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
Organized by the Part that best prepares you to answer each one. Practicing the reasoning, not memorizing the answer, is the point — every question below maps to a worked example earlier in this manual.
## Fundamentals (Parts 1–3)
What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and why can't you filter on an aggregate in WHERE? (2.1, 3.2)
## Why does WHERE column <> 1 sometimes exclude rows you expected to see? (2.3)
## What's the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column), and COUNT(DISTINCT column)? (3.1)
Why is WHERE column = NULL always false, and what should you write instead? (2.3)
```sql
Explain the logical order of execution of a SQL query's clauses (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY). Why can't you use a SELECT alias in a WHERE clause? (1.3)
```
What happens if you GROUP BY one column but SELECT another column that isn't aggregated? (3.2)
Joins (Part 4)
```sql
Explain the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and FULL OUTER JOIN, with an example of when each would give a different row count. (4.1)
```
How would you find all rows in table A that have no matching row in table B? Give two different ways to write it. (4.1, 5.3)
## What is "fan-out" in a join, and how can it silently produce a wrong SUM or COUNT? (4.1)
## What's a self join, and give a real-world example of when you'd need one. (4.2)
Why doesn't ON a.col = b.col match two rows that both have NULL in that column? (4.1, 2.3)
## Subqueries, CTEs, sets (Part 5)
## What's the difference between a correlated and an uncorrelated subquery? (5.1)
Why can NOT IN silently return zero rows when the subquery contains a NULL? What's the safer alternative? (2.3, 5.1)
## What is a CTE, and how is it different from a derived table (subquery in FROM)? (5.2)
What's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and why would you default to UNION ALL? (5.4)
```sql
Explain what a window function does that a GROUP BY cannot. Give an example using ROW_NUMBER(). (5.5)
```
How would you find the "top N per group" (e.g., the top 3 highest earners per department)? (5.5)
## Data validation & QA-specific (Parts 6, 10)
You're told a data migration "passed" because the row counts matched on both sides. Why might that still hide serious bugs? (6.1)
How would you find duplicate records in a table where duplicates are defined by a combination of columns, not a single one? (3.2, 6.3)
Describe how you'd validate that a computed/aggregated dashboard number is correct, without trusting the application's own calculation. (6.2, 9.3)
## What's the difference between a "hard" orphan record and a "logical" orphan record? (4.3)
How would you design a reusable SQL-based sanity check suite for a QA team? What makes a check "good"? (10.2)
Given a status column and a status_history table, how would you check that the current status always matches the latest history entry? (6.3, 10.5)
## Constraints & schema (Part 8)
What's the difference between a UNIQUE constraint and a PRIMARY KEY? Can a unique column contain NULL? (8.1)
```sql
Explain what an index does and why adding more indexes isn't always better. (8.1, 8.5)
```
What test cases would you write just from reading a column definition of VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL? (8.2)
What's a "soft delete," and what's the classic bug it introduces with unique constraints? (4.3, 8.4)
## Transactions & concurrency (Part 7)
What does ACID stand for, and give a concrete example of an atomicity failure in a real application. (7.7)
## What is a "lost update," and how would you test for one? (7.7)
## What's the difference between a deadlock and a lock wait timeout? (7.7)
Why can't you always test a multi-step API operation's atomicity by just checking the final HTTP response? (7.3, 9.1)
## Practical / scenario-based
Write a query to find employees who have never submitted a leave request. (Multiple valid approaches: NOT IN with a NULL guard, NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL, or EXCEPT — 5.1, 5.3, 5.4)
A report shows a total that doesn't match the sum of the rows displayed underneath it. Walk through how you'd investigate. (9.6, 11.3)
You need to test that deleting a department with active employees is properly blocked. How would you set this up and verify it, including at the database level? (4.3, 8.1)
Given access to a database you've never seen before, describe your first hour of exploration. (8.6)
How would you performance-test a slow report, and what would you look for in an EXPLAIN plan? (8.5)
```sql
Explain how you'd verify PII is properly masked in a QA environment copied from production. (7.6)
```
